author: Carlos Martinez
title: The Dallara IR-18 IndyCar on iRacing: Speed That Changes How You Brake
description: My honest impressions racing the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar on iRacing — setup notes, wheel feel, and who this car actually suits.

sections.p: I run all of this from a fixed-aluminium-extrusion cockpit with a ~MOZA R9 direct drive wheelbase and ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals — no motion, no fancy paint, just a rig built to be honest about what the car is doing. Here's what the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar has actually been like to race, across the tracks I run most — not a spec-sheet rundown, just what I've actually noticed after enough laps to trust my own impressions.

I try to give a car a genuinely fair chance before forming an opinion on it — a session or two of just getting comfortable before I start comparing it to anything else I race. The Dallara IR-18 IndyCar is a good example of a car that rewarded that patience; my first impression and my impression after a few weeks weren't quite the same.

sections.h2: What this car is really like to drive

sections.p: The aero load at speed is unlike anything else I regularly race — braking points that would be laughably early in a GT3 car are exactly right here once the car is loaded up with downforce.

That character shows up most clearly once you're pushing near the limit rather than cruising around at seven-tenths — which is honestly true of most race cars, but it's worth saying plainly here because a lot of first impressions of the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar get formed in that first cautious session and then never get revisited.

list: Front and rear wing balance is one of the most consequential setup choices in the whole car, more so than in most GT3s I run
I pay much closer attention to aero balance shifting as I follow another car closely — dirty air affects the IR-18 noticeably more than a GT3 car
Gearing has to account for a genuinely wide speed range between road-course corners and oval configurations

sections.p: As with any setup notes, I'd treat these as a starting direction rather than a fixed recipe — track-specific demands, personal preference, and even the specific series rules you're racing under can all shift what actually works best. Change one thing at a time and judge it against a stopwatch, not just a feeling.

sections.h2: How it feels through the wheel

sections.p: At speed, the ~MOZA R9 telegraphs the aero load building progressively as the car accelerates — it's one of the clearest examples I've felt of downforce as a physical sensation rather than just a setup number on a page.

Pedal feel matters just as much here as wheel feel, and I'd say the same logic applies to the ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals I run — a car's braking character comes through in how the pedal resists your foot, not just in how the car decelerates on screen. Cars with different weight distributions like the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar genuinely reward paying attention to that resistance curve rather than just stomping to a fixed travel point every time.

sections.tip: Give yourself more laps than usual to recalibrate your braking points when you first jump into the IR-18 — your GT3 muscle memory will brake early almost everywhere at first.

sections.h2: Common mistakes I see (and made myself) in this car

list: Carrying over setup habits from a different car class instead of respecting what the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar specifically rewards
Judging the car's limit too early, in the first session, before tires and the driver are both actually warmed up
Ignoring how the car's character changes over a longer run as tires wear, rather than just tuning for a single fast lap

sections.p: Drivers who want to experience genuinely high aero loads and a different braking rhythm than GT racing, and anyone curious about oval and road-course versions of the same chassis.

sections.h2: Practice plan for getting comfortable with this car

olist: Spend a full session with no other cars on track just learning where the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar's grip limit actually is in isolation
Run a handful of laps intentionally over the limit in a low-stakes session so you know what the car's warning signs feel like before you're relying on avoiding them under race pressure
Do at least one longer run at race pace rather than qualifying pace before your first real race in the car, so tire wear and fuel load aren't a surprise
Race it in a lower-pressure series first if you can, before bringing it into a series or split where the stakes and traffic density are higher

sections.p: That progression matters more with the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar than it might with a car you're already deeply familiar with, simply because every car has its own specific way of warning you before it lets go, and you can't actually learn that warning from reading about it — only from spending time right at the edge of it in a controlled setting.

sections.h2: What I'd change about my own approach next time

sections.p: Looking back at my early sessions in the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar, I spent too long trying to force a setup and driving style that worked well in a different car onto it, rather than treating it as its own thing with its own demands from lap one. That cost me more time than any actual mechanical shortcoming in the car itself, and it's a mistake I think a lot of drivers make whenever they change car class — old habits are comfortable, but comfortable isn't the same as correct for the car you're actually in.

If I were starting over with this car today, I'd spend the first full session purely on getting comfortable with its specific braking and rotation character before touching the setup at all — changing the car's balance before you actually understand its default behavior just muddies the feedback you're trying to learn from.

sections.h2: A quick note on iRating and Safety Rating in this car

sections.p: Jumping into a new car class, including the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar, resets some of your comfort even if your iRating and Safety Rating carry over. I'd expect a small dip in results for the first several races purely from unfamiliarity, and I wouldn't read too much into it — it's a normal, temporary cost of learning something new, not a sign you've actually gotten worse at racing in general.

If you're deciding what to race next, it's worth reading my notes on tyre temps and pressures too — car choice and track choice both matter more than people give them credit for when you're building consistency, and the two decisions usually aren't independent of each other.

faqs.q: Is the Dallara IR-18 IndyCar good for a driver moving up in car class?
faqs.a: Generally yes, provided the jump in grip and speed from your current car isn't too large — I'd recommend a session or two of just getting comfortable before pushing for outright pace.

faqs.q: What wheelbase do you race this car on?
faqs.a: I run a ~MOZA R9 with ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals for all my iRacing sessions, including this car.

faqs.q: Do the setup notes here apply across all tracks?
faqs.a: They're a starting point rather than a fixed answer — I adjust from this baseline depending on the specific track's demands.
That depends on your current experience level more than the car itself — see the 'who this car suits' section above for my honest take.
